newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate ratifies changes to European arms accord.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate ratifies changes to European arms accord.

text.p: The U.S. Senate on Wednesday unanimously ratified changes in a European military forces treaty that were negotiated to adapt to the breakup of the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact.
The so-called "flank agreement" to the Conventional Forces in Europe Treaty was approved unanimously despite the Clinton administration's strong objections to a condition added by the Senate.

Massachusetts Democratic Sen. John Kerry accused Republicans of holding the treaty "hostage" to a requirement that President Bill Clinton submit for its approval expansion of the Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) treaty to cover the post-Cold War successors to the former Soviet Union.

But Sen. Bob Smith, a Republican from New Hampshire, argued on the Senate floor that the addition of countries to the ABM treaty demanded Senate action. "Of course it is a substantive change. We have three new nations who had no part in this treaty," he said.

The administration, while objecting to the restrictions on its authority, had urged the Senate to act quickly on the CFE treaty because after May 15, 1997, the modifications would be open to further review by countries who had signed the original 1990 document.

The ratification came as Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin announced a new agreement between former Cold War foes NATO and Russia designed to ease Russian concerns over the expansion of the Western alliance into the formerly communist East.
The changes to the CFE respond to Russian concerns that treaty constraints on its deployment of conventional weapons restricted its ability to meet security requirements in the north Caucasus.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said the treaty addressed one of his concerns in that it granted no additional rights for Russian military deployments outside its borders.

In addition, he said, it contains a provision that ensures the United States will not tacitly support Russian policies that undermine the independence of the Ukraine, Georgia, Moldova and Azerbaijan. And, he noted, it adds inspections and reviews.

While the administration considered the flank agreement as a mere amendment to an existing treaty, it agreed to seek Senate approval as part of a deal to win Senate passage of the chemical weapons treaty.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who has been working on the expansion of NATO, noted the CFE will be the only vehicle to set binding limits on conventional forces in Europe as it is adapted with central European countries and other signatories.
